rationale: A wins because it does the founder's actual pre-pitch job: it separates four usable desks and tells you exactly what must be proven before anyone starts emailing reporters. Its line, "vague \"new revenue stream\" language will not survive an analyst's read," is the adult in the room. B is cleaner on the page, but "Rivian just bet that an exclusive charging network isn't worth keeping" imports a moat thesis the update does not prove. Good angle shape, shaky footing; that is how smart pitches get themselves in trouble.
gaps_in_A: "Every new Rivian stall will carry both plugs — the connector fight is over" is too cute and too big. One dual-connector commitment does not end a connector fight.
"joining the small set of automaker-owned networks that sell to non-owners" imports market context not provided in the update. Fine if sourced, not fine as a blind generated angle.
"competing for the same drivers rather than negotiating with their manufacturers" pushes past "no partnership announced." The set later catches this, but the kept angle still leans on the inference.
The first counterposition angle overlaps a bit with the standards/network angle; it needs a sharper protagonist than "the charging map" to avoid becoming category mush.
gaps_in_B: "Rivian just bet that an exclusive charging network isn't worth keeping" overstates intent. Opening for revenue and utilization does not prove Rivian concluded exclusivity failed.
"The prevailing belief: a proprietary fast-charging network is a moat" is an outside premise, not a supplied fact. That may be true, but the update did not give it to you.
"what it says about the moat thesis the rest of the industry still holds" is unsupported and broad. That is columnist scaffolding pretending to be evidence.
The proof lists are solid but thinner than A's; B does not press hard enough on subset risk, geographic spread, session mechanics, or whether charging revenue is material enough for a markets desk.
